O P E R A T I O N A L S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y
Resource
Management
Energy Efficiency · Water Conservation · Waste Reduction · Circular Economy Principles
01

The global economy is only 6.9% circular.
The other 93% is resources used once, then lost.
Today is entirely practical: the actual calculations engineers and facility managers use to cut energy, water, and waste 
— and the systems-level thinking that ties them together.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 02

T O D A Y ' S J O U R N E Y
Four Resources, One Systems Problem
01
Energy Efficiency
Doing the same work with less power —
and calculating whether it pays for itself.
02
Water Conservation
Protecting the resource India is running 
out of fastest.
03
Waste Reduction
The hierarchy of what to do with 
material before it becomes garbage.
04
The Circular Economy
The systems-level model that ties all 
three together permanently.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Energy Efficiency
Delivering the same output, service, or comfort — while using measurably less power.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Energy Efficiency?
A precise engineering concept, often confused with its cousin, energy conservation.
The Working Definition Using less energy to provide the same product, service, or level of comfort — doing the same job, with less 
input.
Efficiency vs. Conservation Conservation reduces energy use by reducing the service itself (turning off a light); efficiency reduces energy use 
while keeping the service the same (a more efficient light, on for the same hours).
Energy Intensity: The Macro View Energy used per unit of economic output (e.g., MJ per unit of GDP) — a country-level indicator of how efficiently 
an economy converts energy into value.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 06

S E C T I O N 1 · W H E R E I T P A Y S O F F
Four Levers of Energy Efficiency
The same underlying logic — do more with less — applied across every major energy-consuming system.
Buildings & HVAC
Insulation, smart thermostats, and 
efficient heating/cooling — buildings 
account for a large share of global energy 
demand.
Industrial Processes
Waste heat recovery, efficient motors, 
and process optimization — often the 
fastest payback in an industrial facility.
Lighting
LED lighting uses a small fraction of the 
energy of incandescent bulbs for the 
same brightness — one of the simplest, 
fastest wins available.
Transport & Logistics
Fuel efficiency standards, route 
optimization, and electrification reduce 
energy use per kilometre travelled.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 07

S E C T I O N 1 · M A K I N G I T S Y S T E M A T I C
ISO 50001: Energy Management Systems
Efficiency gains stick when they're built into a management system — not left to one-off projects.
What It Is The international standard for establishing, implementing, and continually improving an energy management 
system within an organization.
The Core Cycle A Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle: set an energy baseline and targets, implement improvements, measure results, and 
adjust — repeated continuously.
Why It Matters It turns "we should save energy" into an auditable, repeatable organizational process — the same logic industrial 
quality systems use for defects.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 08

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Payback Period on an LED Lighting Retrofit
G I V E N
200 incandescent bulbs (60 W each), operating 10 hours/day
Replacing with 200 LED bulbs (9 W each)
Electricity cost: ₹7/kWh; Retrofit cost: ₹250/bulb (₹50,000 total)
F O R M U L A
Payback Period (years) = Total Investment ÷ Annual Cost Savings
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Power saved per bulb: 60W − 9W = 51W = 0.051 kW
2 Daily savings (200 bulbs): 0.051 kW × 10 hrs × 200 = 102 kWh/day → 37,230 kWh/year
3 Annual cost savings: 37,230 kWh × ₹7/kWh = ₹2,60,610/year
4 Payback: ₹50,000 ÷ ₹2,60,610 ≈ 0.19 years ≈ 2.3 months
≈ 2.3 Months The retrofit pays for itself in under three months — incandescent-to-LED conversions are among the fastest-payback efficiency 
investments that exist.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 09

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"Of the four levers — buildings, industry, lighting, 
transport — which do you think offers the fastest 
payback for a typical Indian college campus, and 
why?"
Think about what's cheapest to retrofit versus what saves the most energy.
3 MIN
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 10

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What is the key difference between energy efficiency and energy 
conservation?
A They are exactly the same thing
B
Efficiency keeps the service the same while using less energy; conservation reduces the 
service itself
C Conservation only applies to industry, efficiency only to buildings
D Efficiency always costs more than conservation
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Efficiency keeps the service the same 
while using less energy; conservation 
reduces the service itself
Energy conservation reduces energy use by reducing 
or eliminating the service (e.g., turning off a light). 
Energy efficiency reduces energy use while keeping 
the exact same service level (e.g., a more efficient 
light, on for the same number of hours) — a subtle but 
important engineering distinction.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
Water Conservation
Protecting the resource that India, specifically, is running out of fastest.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E U R G E N C Y
India's Water Stress, By The Numbers
~600 M
Indians facing high to extreme water 
stress (NITI Aayog, CWMI)
820 M
People live in river basins with per 
capita availability at or below the 
scarcity threshold
1,486 m³
India's per capita water availability 
(2021), projected to fall toward 1,140 
m³ by 2050
18% / 4%
Share of world's population India 
holds, versus share of world's 
freshwater resources
India's water demand is projected to be twice its available supply by 2030 — an estimated 6% loss of GDP if unaddressed.
Source: NITI Aayog, Composite Water Management Index (CWMI); Ministry of Jal Shakti.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 13

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E T O O L K I T
Four Tools for Water Conservation
Interventions available at every scale, from a single building to an entire watershed.
Low-Flow Fixtures
Efficient taps, showerheads, and dual￾flush toilets can cut household and 
institutional water use significantly with 
no change in service.
Rainwater Harvesting
Capturing rooftop and surface runoff for 
direct use or groundwater recharge —
cheap, decentralized, and highly 
effective at scale.
Wastewater Recycling
Treating and reusing greywater and 
treated sewage for irrigation, cooling, or 
flushing — reducing demand on 
freshwater sources.
Precision Irrigation
Drip and micro-irrigation target water 
directly at crop roots — critical since 
agriculture consumes roughly 85% of 
India's water use.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 14

S E C T I O N 2 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Calculating Rainwater Harvesting Potential
G I V E N
Rooftop catchment area: 500 m²
Average annual rainfall in the region: 900 mm (0.9 m)
Runoff coefficient for a concrete roof: 0.85 (85% collection efficiency)
F O R M U L A
Harvestable Water (litres) = Area (m²) × Rainfall (m) × Runoff 
Coefficient × 1000
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Volume of rain falling on the roof: 500 m² × 0.9 m = 450 m³
2 Apply the runoff coefficient: 450 m³ × 0.85 = 382.5 m³
3 Convert to litres: 382.5 × 1,000 = 3,82,500 litres
3.83 Lakh L/Year This single rooftop can realistically harvest nearly 4 lakh litres of water annually — enough to meaningfully offset a building's 
freshwater demand.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 15

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E N A T I O N A L R E S P O N S E
Jal Shakti Abhiyan
India's flagship national water conservation campaign, launched in 2019.
The Mandate A time-bound, mission-mode campaign focused on water-stressed districts, run jointly by central and state 
governments.
The Five Focus Areas Water conservation and rainwater harvesting; renovation of traditional water bodies; reuse and recharge 
structures; watershed development; and intensive afforestation.
Why It Matters Here It operationalizes the exact interventions in this section — rainwater harvesting, recharge, and precision water 
management — at national scale.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 16

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Roughly what share of India's total water use goes to agriculture, 
making precision irrigation such a high-leverage intervention?
A About 25%
B About 50%
C About 85%
D About 10%
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. About 85%
Agriculture accounts for roughly 85% of India's total 
water consumption, primarily through irrigation —
making even modest efficiency gains from drip and 
precision irrigation enormously significant at national 
scale.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 17

S E C T I O N 3 O F 4
Waste Reduction
The hierarchy of what to do with material — long before it becomes something to throw away.
18

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E C O R E F R A M E W O R K
The Waste Hierarchy
Not all waste management options are equal — this hierarchy ranks them from most to least preferred.
1. Refuse & Reduce Avoid creating the waste in the first place — the only tier that eliminates impact entirely.
2. Reuse Use a product again, in its original form, for the same or a different purpose.
3. Recycle Break a material down and remanufacture it into something new.
4. Recover Extract energy from waste that cannot be reused or recycled (e.g., waste-to-energy).
5. Dispose Landfill — the least preferred option, used only when nothing else is possible.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 19

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Calculating a City's Landfill Diversion Rate
G I V E N
A city generates 1,000 tonnes of municipal solid waste per day
Of this: 350 tonnes is composted, 150 tonnes is recycled
The remaining 500 tonnes goes to landfill
F O R M U L A
Diversion Rate (%) = (Waste Diverted from Landfill ÷ Total Waste 
Generated) × 100
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Total waste diverted: composted + recycled = 350 + 150 = 500 tonnes
2 Diversion rate: (500 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 50%
50% Diversion Exactly half of this city's waste is being kept out of the landfill — the standard metric cities and campuses use to track waste
management progress.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 20

S E C T I O N 3 · W H O P A Y S F O R E N D - OF - L I F E
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
A policy principle that shifts the cost and responsibility for waste back onto the companies that created it.
The Core Idea Producers are made financially and physically responsible for the end-of-life management of the products and 
packaging they place on the market.
India's E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 Mandate producers of electronics to meet specific e-waste collection and recycling targets, obtained through 
registered recyclers.
India's Plastic Waste Management Rules Require producers, importers, and brand owners of plastic packaging to meet EPR targets for collection and 
recycling.
Why It Changes Behaviour When producers bear disposal costs, they have a direct financial incentive to design products that are easier and 
cheaper to recycle.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 21

◆ INTERACTIVE C L A S S I F Y T H E A C T I O N
Where Does This Sit in the Waste Hierarchy?
For each real action, decide which tier of the waste hierarchy it belongs to.
1 Refilling a glass bottle instead of buying a new one
2 Melting down aluminium cans to make new cans
3 Sending unsorted mixed waste directly to a landfill
4 Designing packaging to use less material from the start
5 Burning non-recyclable waste to generate electricity
6 Donating used furniture instead of throwing it away
REDUCE/REUSE RECYCLE/RECOVER DISPOSE
1 2 3
4 5
6
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 22

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Under Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), who is made 
financially responsible for a product's end-of-life management?
A The consumer who purchased the product
B The local municipal government
C The producer or brand owner who placed the product on the market
D Recycling companies exclusively
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. The producer or brand owner who 
placed the product on the market
EPR shifts responsibility for end-of-life management —
collection, recycling, safe disposal — back onto the 
producer or brand owner, creating a direct financial 
incentive to design products that are easier and 
cheaper to recycle.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 23

S E C T I O N 4 O F 4
The Circular Economy
The systems-level model that ties energy, water, and waste together — permanently, not as separate projects.
24

S E C T I O N 4 · T H E F R A M E W O R K
Three Principles of a Circular Economy
As defined by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation — the most widely cited framework in the field.
Design Out Waste & Pollution Waste is treated as a design flaw, not an inevitability — products and systems are designed from the outset to 
prevent it.
Keep Products & Materials in Use Through reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and recycling — extending value for as long as physically possible.
Regenerate Natural Systems Circular systems actively rebuild natural capital — returning nutrients to soil, restoring ecosystems — not just 
minimizing harm.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 25

S E C T I O N 4 · T W O K I N D S O F C I R C U L A T I O N
The Technical Cycle vs. the Biological Cycle
The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's "butterfly diagram" splits circularity into two distinct loops, based on what kind of material is involved.
The Technical Cycle
Applies to durable, manufactured materials: metals, plastics, glass, electronics.
Circulates through maintenance, reuse, refurbishment, remanufacturing, and 
recycling.
Goal: keep the material in a manufactured loop indefinitely, never returning to 
raw extraction.
The Biological Cycle
Applies to renewable, biodegradable materials: food waste, natural fibers, 
wood.
Circulates through composting and anaerobic digestion, safely returning 
nutrients to the soil.
Goal: regenerate natural systems, not just avoid landfill.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 26

S E C T I O N 4 · W H E R E T H E W O R L D A C T U A L L Y S T A N D S
The Circularity Gap
6.9%
The share of materials in the global economy that are 
cycled back — down from 9.1% in 2018
93.1%
Share of all materials entering the global economy that 
still come from virgin extraction
€25.4 Tn
The "Value Gap": economic value lost annually to 
linear resource use — nearly 31% of global GDP
Despite two decades of circular economy advocacy, the world has gotten measurably less circular, not more — the gap is the opportunity.
Source: Circle Economy & Deloitte, Circularity Gap Report 2025 & 2026.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 27

S E C T I O N 4 · W H E R E T H E V A L U E A C T U A L L Y L E A K S
The Five Pathways of Value Loss
The Circularity Gap Report 2026 breaks the €25.4 trillion Value Gap into five specific leaks in the system.
End-of-Life Waste (€10.0 
Tn)
The single largest leak: 
products landfilled or 
incinerated instead of 
refurbished, reused, or 
recycled.
Energy Losses (€8.7 Tn)
Energy lost during raw 
material extraction, inefficient 
grid transmission, and poor 
thermal regulation in 
buildings.
Food Losses & Waste
Edible food lost across 
production, distribution, and 
consumption before it ever 
reaches — or after it leaves —
a plate.
Processing Losses
Material lost as offcuts, scrap, 
and by-products during 
manufacturing that are never 
captured or reused.
Premature Deterioration
Buildings, infrastructure, and 
equipment retired or replaced 
well before the end of their 
useful physical life.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 28

◆ INTERACTIVE C L A S S I F Y T H E M A T E R I A L
Technical Cycle or Biological Cycle?
For each material, decide which of the two circular economy loops it belongs to.
1 Aluminium cans
2 Food scraps and vegetable peels
3 Smartphone components
4 Garden and yard waste
5 Glass bottles
6 Untreated wood offcuts
TECHNICAL CYCLE BIOLOGICAL CYCLE
1 2
3 4
5 6
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 29

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
According to the Circularity Gap Report, what is the single largest of 
the five pathways of value loss in the global economy?
A Food losses and waste
B Processing losses
C End-of-life waste
D Premature deterioration of buildings
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. End-of-life waste
End-of-life waste — products landfilled or incinerated 
instead of refurbished, reused, or recycled — is the 
largest single pathway of value loss, estimated at 
roughly €10.0 trillion annually in the Circularity Gap 
Report 2026.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 30

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
One Systems Problem, Not Four Separate Ones
Energy, water, and waste are not independent projects — the circular economy is the framework that shows why.
Energy Efficiency Reduces the energy embedded in every material extracted, processed, and moved — the "energy losses" pathway in the Value 
Gap.
Water Conservation Recycled water and precision irrigation are themselves circular loops — keeping a resource in use instead of extracting more.
Waste Reduction The waste hierarchy is a miniature version of the circular economy — refuse and reuse before recycle, recycle before dispose.
The Circular Economy The framework that shows these three are not separate initiatives — they are one system, viewed from three different points.
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 31

◆ INTERACTIVE A P P L Y I T A L L
"Pick a building or campus you know well. Where 
would you find the fastest-payback energy fix, the 
biggest water-saving opportunity, and the worst 
waste leak — all three?"
This is exactly how a resource management audit actually starts.
4 MIN
RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 32

O P E R A T I O N A L S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y
Sustainable
Supply Chains
Integrating environmental considerations into sourcing, production, and distribution
01

You already know 70–90% of a company's footprint lives in its 
supply chain.
Today is about what to actually do about it.
Three stages — sourcing, production, distribution — and the specific interventions, standards, and case studies that 
make each one measurably more sustainable.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 02

Following the Product, Upstream to Downstream
Sustainable Supply Chain Management (SSCM): integrating environmental and social criteria into every decision along a product's journey — not just at the factory 
gate.
01
Sourcing
Where raw materials come from, and 
under what conditions.
02
Production
How materials become products — and 
at what environmental cost.
03
Distribution
How products move to market — often 
the most visible emissions of all.
04
Measuring the Chain
Mapping, tracking, and reporting the 
whole system end to end.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Sustainable Sourcing
Where raw materials come from, and under what conditions — the origin point of most supply chain risk.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Sustainable Sourcing?
The furthest-upstream link in the chain — and, per the GHG Protocol, usually the largest share of a company's real footprint.
The Working Definition Procuring raw materials and components in ways that account for environmental impact, labor conditions, and 
long-term resource availability — not price alone.
Why Upstream Matters Most Categories 1 and 4 of Scope 3 (purchased goods, upstream transportation) are frequently a company's single 
largest emissions category — often larger than its own operations.
The Core Challenge A company rarely owns its suppliers — sustainable sourcing means influencing behavior it cannot directly 
control, several tiers removed from its own operations.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 06

S C O P E 3 : C a t e g o r i e s :
Upstream Scope 3 — Categories 1 to 8
Everything that happens before a product or service reaches your organization.
1. Purchased Goods & Services
Emissions from producing everything your 
organization buys or acquires.
2. Capital Goods
Emissions from producing purchased long￾term assets — machinery, buildings, 
equipment.
3. Fuel- & Energy-Related Activities
Upstream emissions of fuel and energy not 
already counted in Scope 1 or 2.
4. Upstream Transportation & 
Distribution
Third-party transport of purchased products 
to your organization.
5. Waste Generated in Operations
Emissions from third-party disposal and 
treatment of your operational waste.
6. Business Travel
Employee travel for business in vehicles not 
owned by the organization — flights, trains, 
taxis.
7. Employee Commuting
Emissions from employees' travel between 
home and work.
8. Upstream Leased Assets
Emissions from operating assets you lease, 
not already in Scope 1 or 2.
CARBON FOOTPRINT CALCULATION · SCOPE 1, 2 & 3 28

S E C T I O N 1 · W H A T C A N G O W R O N G
Four Categories of Sourcing Risk
The specific failure modes that make upstream sourcing the riskiest link in most supply chains.
Deforestation-Linked 
Commodities
Palm oil, soy, cattle, and timber are 
consistently linked to tropical 
deforestation when sourced without 
traceability.
Conflict Minerals
Tin, tungsten, tantalum, and gold 
sourced from conflict-affected regions 
can finance armed groups and human 
rights abuses.
Forced & Child Labour
Complex, multi-tier supply chains can 
obscure labor abuses far removed from 
the buying company's direct view.
Biodiversity & Habitat Loss
Extraction of raw materials — mining, 
fishing, logging — can degrade 
ecosystems far from where the final 
product is sold.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 07

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E R E S P O N S E
Certifications That Address Sourcing Risk
Third-party certification is the primary tool buyers use to verify claims they cannot check themselves.
Fairtrade
Certifies fair prices and labor standards 
for commodities like coffee, cocoa, and 
cotton, verified by independent audit.
Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)
Certifies wood and paper products from 
responsibly managed forests, with full 
chain-of-custody tracking.
Rainforest Alliance
Certifies farms meeting environmental, 
social, and economic sustainability 
criteria, common in coffee, tea, and 
cocoa.
Responsible Minerals Initiative
Audits smelters and refiners to verify 
minerals are not sourced from conflict￾affected or high-risk areas.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 08

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When Sourcing Oversight Fails: Rana Plaza
The Rana Plaza Collapse, Dhaka, Bangladesh (April 24, 2013)
An eight-story building housing five garment factories collapsed, killing 1,134 workers and injuring approximately 2,500 more — the deadliest disaster in the 
history of the garment industry.
The Sourcing Failure
The factories supplied major global apparel brands, whose supplier audits had never 
identified the building's fundamental structural defects.
The Warning Ignored
Visible cracks were discovered the day before the collapse; workers were ordered back to 
their 13–14 hour shifts regardless.
The Systemic Response
The legally binding Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh was signed within a 
month by over 200 global brands and retailers.
The Lesson
Supplier audits that check labor and quality standards, but not structural safety, can miss 
the most catastrophic risks entirely.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 09

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"A brand's supplier audit checks fire exits and pay 
stubs, but not structural engineering. What other 
kinds of 'invisible' risk might a standard audit 
checklist miss today?"
Think beyond garments — electronics, food, minerals.
3 MIN
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 10

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
For most companies, which GHG Protocol Scope 3 categories are 
most directly addressed by sustainable sourcing practices?
A Category 11 (Use of sold products) and Category 12 (End-of-life)
B Category 1 (Purchased goods & services) and Category 4 (Upstream transportation)
C Category 6 (Business travel) only
D Sourcing has no connection to Scope 3 at all
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Category 1 (Purchased goods & services) 
and Category 4 (Upstream transportation)
Sustainable sourcing addresses the upstream 
categories of Scope 3 most directly — Category 1 
(purchased goods & services) and Category 4 
(upstream transportation) — which are frequently a 
company's single largest emissions categories.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
Sustainable Production
How raw materials become products — and the environmental cost embedded in every design choice.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Sustainable Production?
Manufacturing that minimizes environmental impact per unit of output — not simply "cleaner factories."
The Working Definition Producing goods using processes and materials that minimize energy use, water use, waste, and toxic emissions 
relative to the value created.
Cleaner Production, Not End-of-Pipe The modern approach prevents pollution and waste at the source — in process and material design — rather 
than treating waste after it's already created.
Why It's a Design Problem The vast majority of a product's environmental impact is locked in at the design stage, long before a single unit is 
manufactured.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 13

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E C O R E T O O L
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)
The standardized method for actually measuring a product's environmental impact — from raw material to disposal.
Cradle-to-Gate Measures impact from raw material extraction through to the factory gate — the boundary most manufacturers 
can measure directly.
Cradle-to-Grave Extends the assessment through use and disposal — the full picture of a product's lifetime impact.
Cradle-to-Cradle Extends further still: designed explicitly so the product's materials become the raw material for the next product 
cycle.
Why It Matters Here LCA is what lets a company compare two production or material choices quantitatively, instead of guessing 
which is "greener."
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 14

S E C T I O N 2 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Comparing Packaging Materials with LCA Thinking
G I V E N
Two packaging options, each weighing 50 g (0.050 kg) per unit
Option A — Virgin plastic: embodied emissions of 3.5 kgCO₂e per kg of 
material produced
Option B — Recycled plastic (rPET): embodied emissions of 1.2 kgCO₂e per kg 
of material produced
F O R M U L A
Embodied Emissions per Unit = Weight (kg) × Emission Factor 
(kgCO₂e/kg)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Option A: 0.050 kg × 3.5 kgCO₂e/kg = 0.175 kgCO₂e per unit
2 Option B: 0.050 kg × 1.2 kgCO₂e/kg = 0.060 kgCO₂e per unit
3 Savings per unit: 0.175 − 0.060 = 0.115 kgCO₂e
4 At 1 million units produced per year: 0.115 kg × 1,000,000 = 115,000 kg = 115 tonnes CO₂e saved
115 t CO₂e / Year A single material substitution — virgin to recycled plastic — saves the equivalent of many households' annual emissions, without
changing the product itself.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 15

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E T O O L K I T
Four Cleaner Production Techniques
Concrete interventions that reduce environmental impact at the point of manufacture.
Energy & Water Efficiency
Optimizing industrial processes to use 
less energy and water per unit of output 
— often the fastest payback in a factory.
Waste Minimization
Redesigning processes to generate less 
scrap, off-cuts, and by-product in the 
first place — not just recycling more of it.
Safer Chemical Substitution
Replacing hazardous solvents, dyes, and 
inputs with less toxic alternatives that 
achieve the same manufacturing result.
Process Optimization
Fine-tuning temperatures, cycle times, 
and equipment settings to cut energy 
and material use without changing the 
product.
SUSTAINABLE SUPPLY CHAINS 16

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What is the key difference between "cradle-to-gate" and "cradle-to￾cradle" in Life Cycle Assessment?
A They measure exactly the same boundary
B
Cradle-to-gate stops at the factory; cradle-to-cradle is designed so end-of-life materials 
become new raw material
C Cradle-to-cradle only applies to food products
D Cradle-to-gate includes disposal, cradle-to-cradle does not
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. Cradle-to-gate stops at the factory; 
cradle-to-cradle is designed so end-of-life 
materials become new raw material
Cradle-to-gate measures impact only up to the factory 
gate. Cradle-to-cradle is the most ambitious boundary 
— the product and its materials are explicitly designed 
to become the raw material for a future product cycle,

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
One Chain, Three Interventions, One Measurement System
Sourcing, production, and distribution are not separate sustainability projects — they are three points on the same value chain, measured by the same framework.
Sustainable Sourcing Reduces risk and impact before a material ever enters the factory — certifications and audits are the tools.
Sustainable Production Reduces impact per unit made — Life Cycle Assessment is the tool that makes design choices comparable.
Sustainable Distribution Reduces impact per unit moved — mode shift is the single highest-leverage lever available.
Measurement & Visibility Ties all three together into one Scope 3 inventory — and is the actual bottleneck most companies face today.

S E C T I O N 1 · W H E R E I T A L L S T A R T E D
A Short History of LCA
The methodology is older than the environmental movement that now relies on it.
1969 — The Coca-Cola Study
Coca-Cola commissioned the Midwest Research Institute to compare glass, plastic, and metal beverage 
containers — a "Resource and Environmental Profile Analysis" (REPA), the acknowledged precursor to modern 
LCA.
1990 — A Formal Definition The Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry (SETAC) formally defined LCA as an objective process for 
evaluating environmental burdens.
1997–2006 — ISO Standardization The ISO 14040 series was first published in 1997 and finalized in its current form (ISO 14040:2006 and ISO 
14044:2006), the global standard used today.
LIFE CYCLE ASSESSMENT (LCA) 06

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E F I R S T P H A S E
What Is Goal & Scope Definition?
The most consequential phase of an LCA — decisions made here shape every number that follows.
Setting the Goal Why is this study being done, and who is the intended audience? A study for internal design decisions differs 
from one meant for public marketing claims.
Setting the Scope What system boundaries, level of detail, and assumptions will the study use? This is where the study's credibility 
is either built or undermined.
Why It Comes First Every later phase depends entirely on choices made here — get the goal and scope wrong, and no amount of 
careful data collection afterward can fix it.
LIFE CYCLE ASSESSMENT (LCA) 07

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E K E Y C O N C E P T
The Functional Unit
The single most important, and most frequently misunderstood, concept in all of LCA.
The Definition A quantified description of the performance a product system delivers — the reference unit that makes fair 
comparison possible.
Why "One Product" Isn't Enough "One hand dryer" and "one paper towel" cannot be compared directly — but "drying one pair of hands, once" 
can. The functional unit must describe the function, not the object.
A Classic Failure Mode
Comparing "one reusable cotton bag" to "one plastic bag" ignores that the cotton bag must be reused dozens or 
hundreds of times to deliver the same function as many single-use bags — the functional unit exposes this 
immediately.
LIFE CYCLE ASSESSMENT (LCA) 08

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Comparing Products via a Shared Functional Unit
G I V E N
Functional unit: "Drying one pair of hands, once"
Option A — Electric dryer: 1.8 kW rating, used for 25 seconds per event
Option B — Paper towel: 2 sheets per event, 10 g CO₂e embodied per sheet
F O R M U L A
Emissions per Functional Unit = Energy or Material Used per Event ×
Emission Factor
(Grid factor used: 0.7 kgCO₂e/kWh)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Dryer energy per event: 1.8 kW × (25 ÷ 3,600) hr = 0.0125 kWh
2 Dryer emissions: 0.0125 kWh × 0.7 kgCO₂e/kWh = 0.00875 kg = 8.75 g CO₂e
3 Paper towel emissions: 2 sheets × 10 g CO₂e/sheet = 20 g CO₂e
8.75 g vs. 20 g In this simplified model, the electric dryer's footprint per use is roughly 2.3× lower than paper towels — a comparison only 
possible because both were reduced to the same functional unit.

From raw material extraction through to

S E C T I O N 2 · W H E R E T H E N U M B E R S C O M E F R O M
Primary vs. Secondary Data
LCA practitioners rarely have direct measurements for every single process — they combine both types of data.
Primary Data Directly measured or metered data from the actual facility or supply chain being studied — the most accurate, 
but the most expensive and time-consuming to collect.
Secondary Data Data from published databases, industry averages, or literature, used to fill gaps where primary data isn't 
available or practical.
Databases in Practice Ecoinvent is the most widely used commercial LCI database worldwide, providing thousands of standardized 
process datasets across industries.
LIFE CYCLE ASSESSMENT (LCA) 14

S E C T I O N 2 · A G E N U I N E M E T H O D O L O G I C A L P R O B L E M
The Allocation Problem
What happens when one process produces more than one useful output?
Example: an oil refinery produces petrol, diesel, and jet fuel from the same barrel of crude oil in one process. How much of the refinery's total emissions 
belongs to each fuel?
Mass Allocation
Split impacts in proportion to the physical mass of each 
co-product — simple, but ignores that products have 
very different economic and functional value.
Economic Allocation
Split impacts in proportion to each co-product's market 
value — reflects why the process exists, but shifts with 
market prices.
System Expansion
Avoid allocation entirely by expanding the system 
boundary to credit the process for displacing an 
alternative product — the ISO-preferred approach, but 
often harder to apply.
LIFE CYCLE ASSESSMENT (LCA) 15

Allocation Problem
Many industrial processes generate multiple useful products.
Suppose a process consumes: 1000 MJ
and produces:
• Product A = 600 kg
• Product B = 400 kg
How should the environmental burden be divided?
This is known as allocation.
Mass allocation: AllocationA = 600/(600+400)=0.60
Therefore: ImpactA=0.60Itotal
Economic allocation
If Product A has substantially greater economic value, allocation can instead be based on revenue.
fA= mA*PA

where P represents price.
Different allocation methods can produce significantly different results. Therefore allocation 
assumptions must be clearly reported and, where appropriate, tested through sensitivity analysis.

Building a Life Cycle Inventory Entry
G I V E N
1,180 kg of raw plastic resin is fed into a process to manufacture 1,000 kg of 
finished product
The process consumes 450 kWh of electricity
Grid emission factor: 0.7 kgCO₂e/kWh
F O R M U L A
Process Scrap = Material Input − Product Output
Process Emissions = Energy Used × Emission Factor
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Scrap generated: 1,180 kg − 1,000 kg = 180 kg of solid waste per 1,000 kg of product
2 Process emissions: 450 kWh × 0.7 kgCO₂e/kWh = 315 kgCO₂e per 1,000 kg of product
3 Per functional unit (1 kg of product): 0.18 kg scrap and 0.315 kgCO₂e — both become entries in the inventory table
0.18 kg + 0.315 kg CO₂e
Per kilogram of product: 0.18 kg of solid waste and 0.315 kg of CO₂e emissions — two concrete inventory entries built directly 
from a simple mass and energy balance.

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E T H I R D P H A S E
What Is Life Cycle Impact Assessment?
The step that turns "2 kg of CO₂ and 0.5 g of SO₂" into something a decision-maker can actually act on.
Classification Sorting each inventory flow into the impact category (or categories) it contributes to — e.g., CO₂ goes into 
"climate change."
Characterization Converting each flow into a common unit within its category using a characterization factor — exactly how GWP 
converts CH₄ and N₂O into CO₂e.
Normalization & Weighting (Optional) Comparing category scores against a reference (e.g., per-capita global impact), and optionally combining 
categories into a single overall score — the most subjective, most debated steps.

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E S C O R E C A R D
Six Major Impact Categories
GWP is the most famous impact category — but a rigorous LCA reports several others in parallel.
Global Warming Potential
Climate change impact, expressed in kg CO₂-equivalent — the 
category covered in depth in our carbon footprint lecture.
Ozone Depletion Potential
Damage to the stratospheric ozone layer, expressed in kg CFC￾11-equivalent.
Acidification Potential
SO₂ and NOx emissions that cause acid rain and ecosystem 
damage, expressed in kg SO₂-equivalent.
Eutrophication Potential
Excess nitrogen and phosphorus causing algal blooms and 
oxygen depletion in water bodies.
Human Toxicity Potential
Potential health effects from chemical exposure across the life 
cycle.
Water Scarcity Footprint
Freshwater consumption weighted by the local water stress of 
where it was withdrawn.

Characterization: From Raw Emissions to One Impact Score
G I V E N
A product's inventory (per functional unit) includes: 2 kg CO₂, 0.01 kg CH₄, and 
0.002 kg N₂O
GWP-100 characterization factors (IPCC AR6): CO₂ = 1, CH₄ = 27, N₂O = 273
F O R M U L A
Impact Score (kgCO₂e) = Σ [Mass of Substance × Characterization 
Factor]
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 CO₂: 2 kg × 1 = 2 kgCO₂e
2 CH₄: 0.01 kg × 27 = 0.27 kgCO₂e
3 N₂O: 0.002 kg × 273 = 0.546 kgCO₂e
4 Total GWP impact score: 2 + 0.27 + 0.546 = 2.816 kgCO₂e
2.816 kg CO₂e
This is literally what "characterization" means in LCIA — the exact same GWP-weighting logic from our carbon footprint 
calculation lecture, now applied inside a formal LCA.

S E C T I O N 4 · A G E N U I N E L Y C O N T E S T E D C A S E
The Paper vs. Plastic Bag Debate
One of the most frequently cited — and frequently misunderstood — LCA results in public discourse.
The Intuitive Assumption
Plastic feels disposable and paper feels natural, so paper bags are widely assumed to be 
the more sustainable choice.
What Multiple LCA Studies Have Found
Producing paper bags is typically far more energy-, water-, and material-intensive than 
producing single-use plastic bags — meaning a paper bag can have a higher climate impact 
per bag manufactured.
The Reusable Bag Twist
Reusable bags (cotton, especially organic cotton) generally have the highest impact to 
manufacture of all — some published LCA studies estimate they must be reused many 
dozens to several thousand times before their total impact matches a single-use plastic bag 
used once.
The Real Lesson
The "obviously greener" choice is frequently wrong when it hasn't been through a rigorous 
functional-unit comparison — this is exactly why LCA exists as a discipline.

Critiques & Limitations of LCA
A rigorous course treats LCA the same way it treated the Triple Bottom Line and shared value: useful, and imperfect.
Data Quality & Availability
Reliable, representative data is expensive and scarce, especially for supply chains in 
developing regions — forcing reliance on generic secondary data.
Subjectivity in Boundary-Setting
Where the system boundary is drawn, and what gets excluded via "cut-off criteria," can 
swing results significantly without technically breaking any rule.
The Allocation Problem, Revisited
As shown in Section 2, three defensible allocation methods can produce three different 
answers for the same co-product system.
"LCA Shopping"
Because so many methodological choices are left to the practitioner, it is possible to select 
assumptions that favor a predetermined conclusion — a real risk when a company funds its 
own study.

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What does ISO 14044 require every LCA report to explicitly disclose, 
to protect against misleading conclusions?
A The exact profit margin of the product studied
B The study's limitations, boundaries, data sources, and key assumptions
C The names of every employee involved in the study
D Nothing — ISO 14044 has no disclosure requirements
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. The study's limitations, boundaries, data 
sources, and key assumptions
ISO 14044 requires transparent disclosure of a study's 
limitations, system boundaries, data quality, and 
assumptions — precisely so that a reader can judge for 
themselves how far to trust the conclusions, and 
detect potential "LCA shopping."
LIFE CYCLE ASSESSMENT (LCA) 31

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
The Four Phases, End to End
Each phase depends entirely on the one before it — and ISO 14044 makes the process explicitly iterative, not strictly linear.
1. Goal & Scope Sets the functional unit and system boundary — every later number is only comparable within this frame.
2. Inventory (LCI) Turns the scope into a quantified list of every input and output, resolving allocation for shared processes.
3. Impact Assessment (LCIA) Classifies and characterizes that inventory into comparable scores across categories like GWP.
4. Interpretation Finds the hotspots, tests the assumptions, and states the limitations — turning numbers into a decision.

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E S H I F T
Why This Is No Longer Optional
Sustainability moved from a philanthropic afterthought to a core strategic and financial concern in roughly two decades.
The Old Model: Compliance & Philanthropy For most of the 20th century, environmental and social action was treated as a cost — regulatory compliance, or 
corporate philanthropy separate from core strategy.
The Turning Point Rising climate litigation, mandatory disclosure regimes (like BRSR and CSRD), extreme weather losses, and ESG￾driven investment flows made sustainability a material financial issue.
The Modern View Boards and CFOs now treat sustainability performance as a genuine input to risk pricing, access to capital, and 
long-term competitiveness — not a side project.

Every major sustainability failure a company faces falls into one of these five buckets.
Regulatory Risk

outright bans on products or

Physical Risk

assets, disrupting supply

Reputational Risk

and greenwashing accusations 
that damage brand trust.
Litigation Risk

regulators, or communities 
over emissions, pollution, or 
misleading claims.
Stranded Asset Risk
Assets that lose most of their 
value before the end of their 
useful life, due to policy or 
market shifts.

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When Risk Actually Materializes: "Dieselgate"
Volkswagen Emissions Scandal (September 2015)
Volkswagen admitted to installing "defeat device" software in roughly 11 million diesel vehicles worldwide, designed to cheat regulatory emissions tests while 
polluting far more on real roads.
Financial Cost
More than $30 billion in fines, penalties, buybacks, and settlements globally — one of the 
largest corporate scandals in history.
Market Reaction
Volkswagen's share price dropped sharply within days of the disclosure, erasing billions in 
market value almost immediately.
Leadership Cost
The CEO resigned within days, and the company's reputation for engineering integrity took 
years to begin repairing.
The Lesson
This started as a regulatory compliance failure — but it became simultaneously a legal, 
financial, and reputational risk, all at once.
